title: The Country Bears
full_review:
How much could a moviegoer expect from a film inspired by an amusement park attraction?

Well, with Disney's silly musical comedy, "The Country Bears," it's pretty much a case of "it is what it is." The idea for the original story came from the Country Bears Jamboree attraction at Walt Disney World, and it is the first of upcoming films to be "inspired" by rides in Disney World. (The next will be the Pirates of the Caribbean.)

In this live-action goof on aging music legends, 11-year-old Beary Barrington (voiced by Haley Joel Osment) is a bear who has been adopted by a human family. But somehow he senses he doesn't fit in, since he looks and acts differently from his parents and brother.

Looking for more folks like himself and his "higher purpose" in life, Beary heads south to Tennessee to the Country Bear Hall, where his favorite band, the Country Bears, got their start. What he finds is that the legendary venue is going to be torn down by the dastardly banker Reed Thimple (Christopher Walken) if $20,000 in back rent isn't paid up.

Beary decides to reunite the band after a decade-long breakup for a benefit concert to save the place. This is no easy feat for the idealistic fan, since the band has been torn apart by old grudges and artistic differences, not to mention too much fame, too much ego and too much honey (which is supposed to be a child-friendly substitute for alcohol).

The animatronic bears, created by the Jim Henson Creature Shop, are distinctive enough with expressive eyes and smooth movements. But they are not as impressive as one would have thought, especially coming from Henson. Yet the voices of the bears are more notable, and the cameos by stars such as Elton John and Queen Latifah and singers Bonnie Raitt, Don Henley and Willie Nelson are an extra treat for the parents.

In a clever scene, Raitt and Henley sit at a bar commenting on how great are the voices of the two bears singing a duet on stage. Naturally, it is Raitt and Henley doing the actual singing. There's also a great musical duel between one of the bears and Brian Setzer of the Stray Cats. And the music itself is a good mixture of country, rock, hip-hop and more.

Derivative of "The Blues Brothers," the story is not as original as it may seem at first. Both movies have some musical misfits (being pursued by cops) who are trying to get their band back together to raise money for some cause.

Also, given the recent string of highly publicized child kidnappings, parents may not appreciate the jocular manner in which a kidnapping subplot is presented: Beary's parents (Stephen Tobolowsky and Meagen Fay) believe that Beary has been snatched, and two bumbling cops are dispatched to try to find Beary. However, while the subplot is woven in to provide some slapstick humor, it seems pretty clear that the intent is not to make fun of such a serious thing as a child kidnapping. Instead, it seems like a case of unfortunate timing.

The predictable plot is secondary to the energetic musical numbers which are upbeat and entertaining. Though he mugs more than acts, Walken, dressed in bowler hat, paisley ascot and blue blazer with a crest on the chest pocket, is fun as the wicked banker with a secret grudge. Alex Rocco also whoops it up as Rip Holland, the Bears' former promoter. Between his goofy dyed hair and comical office location, he's one of the funnier characters in the movie.

All in all, "The Country Bears" is passable entertainment that is likely suitable for older children.

Due to some mild menace, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is G -- general audiences.

- - -

Navarro is on the staff of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' Office for Film and Broadcasting.
